Cape Canaveral LC-36B, 1971-05-30. Twin to Mariner 8 (lost in the Atlantic three weeks earlier when its Centaur failed). Mariner 9 alone carried the orbital science load originally split across the pair — a single spacecraft to map the entire planet from orbit, the first attempt of its kind.
Centaur D-1A upper stage burn places Mariner 9 on a 167-day Type-I transfer to Mars.
First mid-course correction, removing the launch dispersion.
Final approach trim. Pin-targeting the periapsis pass for the MOI burn.
1971-11-14. Mariner 9 closed on Mars to find the entire planet shrouded in the largest global dust storm in recorded observation — only the four Tharsis volcano summits poked through the haze.

15-minute burn of its liquid-fuelled main engine at 00:18 UT 1971-11-14 placed Mariner 9 into a 1398 × 17,917 km, 64.4°-inclination orbit — the first spacecraft of any nation to orbit another planet, beating Soviet Mars 2 by 13 days. The storm cleared by January; over the next 11 months Mariner 9 returned 7,329 images covering ~85% of the Martian surface, discovering Olympus Mons (the largest volcano in the solar system), Valles Marineris (the canyon system that bears its name), and the first close-ups of Phobos + Deimos.

1972-10-27. Mariner 9 ran out of attitude-control gas. Powered down in a parking orbit; NASA expected it to stay in orbit for at least 50 years, with re-entry estimated around 2020–2022 — whether it has already re-entered is unknown.
First spacecraft to orbit another planet

Mariner 9 made every orbiter that followed possible. After a 15-minute MOI burn placed it into Mars orbit on 1971-11-14, the planet below was unrecognisable — a global dust storm had hidden everything except the four Tharsis volcano summits. JPL waited it out. Through January 1972 the dust settled and Mariner 9 returned 7,329 images covering ~85% of the Martian surface, revealing Olympus Mons (the largest volcano in the solar system), Valles Marineris (the canyon system that bears its name), dried river channels suggesting an ancient liquid era, and the first close-ups of Phobos and Deimos. The mission ended 1972-10-27 when attitude-control gas ran out; the spacecraft was expected to stay in orbit for decades; whether it has since re-entered is unknown.
